claims.text: High configurational entropy in multielement nanoparticles increases the spread of local bond strengths.
A wider distribution of local bond strengths retards surface-atom diffusion.
A wider distribution of local bond strengths retards nucleation of the liquid phase.
High-entropy nanoparticles begin premelting and melting later than binary or monometallic nanoparticles.
HEA nanoparticles containing at least five elements can be synthesized on granular supports.
The proposed HEA nanoparticles are near-equimolar and have a narrowly controlled diameter of approximately 2–5 nm.
The controlled comparison varies composition complexity while holding particle size, support loading, support type, and synthesis parameters constant.
Both nanoparticle sets will undergo identical in situ thermal ramps under a controlled atmosphere.
Diversified local bonding environments suppress coordinated surface diffusion in HEA nanoparticles.
Synergy among multiple metal species produces a broad range of local cohesive energies.
A broad range of local cohesive energies inhibits uniform surface melting.
The cocktail effect creates irregular bonding and sites with higher binding energy.
Irregular bonding and higher-binding-energy sites stabilize HEA nanoparticles against thermally driven atomic rearrangement and coalescence.
Surface disordering and coalescence will occur at higher temperatures in HEA nanoparticles than in binary or monometallic controls.
Surface effects dominate the relevant behavior for nanoparticles smaller than approximately 10 nm.
The hypothesis is restricted to supports that provide physical anchoring without significant chemical interaction.
The premelting-temperature shift and stability enhancement depend on the element combination and degree of mixing.
Nanoparticle–support interactions may modify premelting and thermal-stability behavior.
Premelting onset, morphology evolution, particle-size evolution, and thermal-ramp curves can be monitored during the proposed experiment.
A lack of a statistically significant delay in premelting or melting, or a lack of differences in coalescence or surface-diffusion rates, would falsify the proposed mechanism.
